chapterName: Early Republic: The Conflict of the Orders - Origins (509-450 BCE)

briefing.title: Rome, 494 BC
paragraphs: Rome, 494 BC. Fifteen years after driving out its last king, the young Republic is run by two consuls elected each year and a Senate of leading men. All of them come from a small circle of aristocratic families called patricians, who alone hold office and know the unwritten law.

Everyone else is a plebeian. Plebeians farm, trade and fill the army, but while they fight, their farms fail and their debts pile up. Now, with enemies on three sides, the soldiers are about to refuse to march.

timelines.name: The Big Moments
timelines.blurb: Four turning points in the early struggle between patricians and plebeians.

events.label: Last king driven out of Rome
events.fact: According to tradition, the Romans then founded a republic led by two yearly consuls and the Senate.

events.label: Plebeians walk out to the Sacred Mount
events.fact: Plebeian soldiers refused to fight and camped on the Mons Sacer, a hill about 5 km (just over three miles) from Rome.

events.label: Lex Publilia: plebs vote by tribe
events.fact: Voting by tribe instead of by curia freed plebeians from their patrician patrons' influence.

events.label: Twelve Tables formally published
events.fact: According to Livy, the laws were engraved on bronze and displayed so every citizen could know them.

timelines.name: From Debt to Written Law
timelines.blurb: Follow the plebeians from a debt crisis to the long end of their struggle.

events.label: Ragged ex-soldier stirs the Forum
events.fact: Livy tells of a veteran ruined by debt and whipped by creditors, whose story enraged the crowd.

events.label: First tribunes of the plebs take office
events.fact: The tribunate was the first office in Rome open to commoners.

events.label: Tribune attacks consuls' power
events.fact: A tribune claimed the consuls were worse than the kings and proposed a commission to limit them.

events.label: Tribunes increased to ten
events.fact: The Senate hoped more tribunes would defuse the campaign for written law.

events.label: Decemvirs take power to write laws
events.fact: All regular offices were suspended and a board of ten men got one year of unchallengeable power.

events.label: Conflict of the Orders ends
events.fact: The struggle between patricians and plebeians lasted from soon after 509 BC until 287 BC.

timelines.name: The Full Struggle
timelines.blurb: Eight steps from the fall of the kings to the fall of the decemvirs.

events.label: Two consuls replace the kings
events.fact: Tradition says the Republic began when the Romans drove out their last king.

events.label: Consul backs creditors' right to jail
events.fact: Instead of easing the debt crisis, a hard-line consul reinforced creditors' power to imprison debtors.

events.label: Menenius tells the fable of the belly
events.fact: According to tradition, his story persuaded the plebeians on the Sacred Mount to negotiate.

events.label: Sacrosanct tribunes first take office
events.fact: Anyone who laid hands on a tribune could be killed without penalty.

events.label: Plebs start voting by tribe
events.fact: The Lex Publilia is seen by historians as the moment the plebeians became politically independent.

events.label: Commission to limit consuls proposed
events.fact: The Senate stalled for five years, pointing to war and plague.

events.label: Laws handed to ten men
events.fact: The decemvirs were given one year to write down Rome's laws.

events.label: Second secession forces decemvirs out
events.fact: Outrage over Verginia's death drove the people to the Aventine and then the Sacred Mount.

trueFalseDecks.name: Strike and Settlement
trueFalseDecks.blurb: From the debt crisis to the first tribunes.

cards.claim: Rome's two consuls were elected for a single year.
cards.why: Power passed to two consuls, chief magistrates elected for one year, and to the Senate.

cards.claim: In the early Republic, plebeians could stand for consul.
cards.why: Only patricians, a small circle of aristocratic families, could stand for office.

cards.claim: In Livy's story, the ragged soldier's farm was burned while he fought the Sabines.
cards.why: Raiders burned his farm while he was away fighting the Sabines, a hill people north-east of Rome.

cards.claim: After the soldier's story spread, a consul cancelled all debts.
cards.why: A hard-line consul did the opposite, issuing decrees reinforcing creditors' right to imprison debtors.

cards.claim: In the first secession of 494 BC, the plebeians camped on the Mons Sacer.
cards.why: They camped on the Mons Sacer, the 'Sacred Mount', about 5 km (just over three miles) from Rome.

cards.claim: Menenius Agrippa was a former consul well liked by ordinary Romans.
cards.why: The Senate chose him to negotiate because the strikers would trust him.

cards.claim: In Menenius's fable, the limbs grew stronger after they stopped feeding the belly.
cards.why: As the belly starved, so did the limbs, and the whole body wasted away.

cards.claim: Tribunes commanded their own troops to protect plebeians.
cards.why: Tribunes commanded no troops; their power rested on an oath making them sacrosanct.

trueFalseDecks.name: Laws and Lawbreakers
trueFalseDecks.blurb: From the Plebeian Council to the fall of the decemvirs.

cards.claim: The Lex Publilia of 471 BC made plebeians vote by tribe rather than by curia.
cards.why: Historians see this as the moment the plebeians became politically independent.

cards.claim: At first, plebiscites were binding on all Romans.
cards.why: At first they bound only plebeians; laws of 449 BC made plebeian decisions binding on all.

cards.claim: According to Livy, envoys went to study the laws of Carthage.
cards.why: Livy says they studied the laws of Athens and other Greek cities, though some scholars doubt it.

cards.claim: Under the Twelve Tables, a debtor had thirty days to pay.
cards.why: After thirty days his creditor could chain him and feed him about 330 g (a pound) of bread a day for sixty days.

cards.claim: The Twelve Tables allowed patricians and plebeians to marry each other.
cards.why: One law banned marriage between patricians and plebeians.

cards.claim: Verginia was killed by Appius Claudius.
cards.why: Tradition says her own father killed her to save her from Appius Claudius.

cards.claim: The second secession of 449 BC forced the decemvirs to resign.
cards.why: Two senators then negotiated and restored the tribunes and the right of appeal.

cards.claim: Official consul lists include men with plebeian family names in the fifth century BC.
cards.why: This is a puzzle, since the post was supposedly closed to plebeians then.

oddOneOut.why: Tribunes, the Plebeian Council and freedom from some debts all came from the settlement of 494 BC. The Twelve Tables came much later, in 449 BC.
The Sabines, Aequi and Volsci were at war with Rome in 494 BC. Athens was the Greek city whose laws Roman envoys reportedly studied.
These were all features of a tribune's power, except troops: tribunes commanded none and relied on their sacred oath.
Three are rules in the Twelve Tables. Voting by tribe came from the Lex Publilia of 471 BC.
Three happened in 449 BC. The number of tribunes was raised to ten earlier, in 457 BC.
reviewFlags: fact-check: The assigned section only covers the 457 BC increase; the three 449 BC events that define the shared property are explained in other sections.

oddOneOut.why: Patricians controlled the consulship, the Senate and the law. The tribunate was the first office open to commoners.
reviewFlags: fact-check: The assigned section never mentions the tribunate, so it cannot explain why the tribunate is the odd one out.

oddOneOut.why: Three are reasons scholars doubt the traditional story. Lasting a thousand years as the basis of Roman law is praise of the Twelve Tables, not a doubt.

whoAmI.name: Leaders and Tyrants
whoAmI.blurb: Three men who shaped the early struggle.

people.name: Sicinius
clues: My followers built simple defences outside the city and waited.
I advised the soldiers to leave Rome together instead of fighting the Sabines, Aequi and Volsci.
The walkout I planned ended on the Mons Sacer, the Sacred Mount.
I was the plebeian leader who masterminded the first secession of 494 BC.

people.name: Menenius Agrippa
clues: I had already served as consul before the plebeians walked out in 494 BC.
Ordinary Romans liked me, so the Senate sent me to negotiate.
I won over the strikers with a story rather than threats.
I told the fable of the limbs that refused to feed the belly.

people.name: Appius Claudius
clues: I sat on the board meant to finish writing Rome's laws.
When our term ended, my colleagues and I refused to step down.
The second secession of 449 BC forced us to resign.
I was the most notorious decemvir, and tradition says I tried to rape Verginia.

whoAmI.name: Voices and Victims
whoAmI.blurb: A heroine, a historian and a tribune.

people.name: Verginia
clues: My father was a respected centurion, an army officer.
The crowd that saw my death rioted, and the anger spread to the army.
My death led to the second secession of 449 BC.
I was the plebeian girl a notorious decemvir tried to seize.

people.name: Livy
clues: Some think I mixed fact and fable and assumed Roman institutions barely changed.
I reported that envoys went to study the laws of Athens.
I told of a ragged former soldier who threw himself into the Forum.
I wrote the fullest account of these years, nearly five centuries later.

people.name: Sicinius
clues: My power rested on a sworn oath, not on soldiers.
Anyone who laid hands on me could be killed without penalty.
Soon after the first tribunes took office in 493 BC, I was added to their number.
I led the walkout that won the plebs their own officials.
